title: Strings, Runes & Bytes
summary: A Go **string** is an immutable, read-only slice of **bytes** — usually UTF-8 encoded text. A **byte** is one 8-bit value (`uint8`); a **rune** is one Unicode code point (`int32`). Understanding the difference between counting bytes and counting characters is the key to handling text correctly.

subtopics.title: A string is immutable bytes
subtopics.explanation: A string value is a small two-word header: a pointer to a read-only byte array and a length in bytes. Because the bytes are immutable, you cannot assign to s[i]; you build new strings instead. len(s) returns the number of BYTES, not characters.

subtopics.title: byte vs rune
subtopics.explanation: A byte is an alias for uint8 — a single 8-bit unit of storage. A rune is an alias for int32 and represents one Unicode code point (one 'character'). ASCII characters fit in one byte; many other characters take 2-4 bytes in UTF-8.
subtopics.example:
var b byte = 'A' // 65
var r rune = '世' // 19990

subtopics.title: UTF-8 encoding
subtopics.explanation: Go source files and string literals are UTF-8. A code point is stored as 1 to 4 bytes. So 'é' or '世' occupy more than one byte, which is why indexing a string by position can land in the middle of a character.

subtopics.title: Ranging over a string
subtopics.explanation: A for...range loop over a string decodes UTF-8 and yields the byte index of each rune plus the rune itself. This is the correct way to iterate characters. Indexing s[i] instead yields a raw byte.
subtopics.example: for i, r := range "a世" { fmt.Println(i, r) } // 0 97 / 1 19990

subtopics.title: Converting []byte and []rune
subtopics.explanation: []byte(s) gives the raw UTF-8 bytes; []rune(s) decodes into code points so len gives the character count. Both conversions copy the data because strings are immutable but slices are mutable.

foundations.overview: In Go, text is stored as a string — an immutable sequence of bytes that is, by convention, UTF-8 encoded. This design is simple and fast, but it means a string's length is measured in bytes, not characters. To work with individual characters you reach for runes (Unicode code points). Knowing when you are dealing with bytes versus runes is what separates correct text handling from off-by-one bugs and mojibake.
foundations.formalDefinition: A string is an immutable, two-word descriptor (a pointer to a read-only byte array and a length in bytes). A byte is an alias for uint8; a rune is an alias for int32 holding a single Unicode code point. String literals are UTF-8 encoded.
foundations.whyItMatters: Almost every program processes text — names, JSON, logs, user input. Treating bytes as characters silently corrupts non-ASCII data, and string immutability shapes how you build and modify text efficiently.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a string as a sealed ribbon of bytes you can read but never alter. A byte is one bead on the ribbon; a rune is a whole letter, which may be spelled out across several beads when the letter isn't plain ASCII.
foundations.runtimePerspective: A string header is 16 bytes on a 64-bit machine (a pointer plus an int length). Because the backing array is read-only, the compiler can safely share string literals and slice substrings without copying. Converting to []byte or []rune, however, must allocate and copy so the result can be mutated.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Parsing HTTP requests, building JSON, validating user input, slicing log lines, counting characters for UI limits, and normalizing Unicode.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct UTF-8 handling means your product works for users in every language; getting it wrong shows up as corrupted names and broken search, which erodes trust in international markets.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Immutability makes strings safe to share across goroutines without copying, but careless string concatenation in loops creates needless allocations; strings.Builder solves that.
foundations.performanceImpact: Substring slicing is O(1) and allocation-free because it shares the backing array. Conversions to []rune are O(n) and allocate. Repeated `+=` concatenation is O(n^2); strings.Builder is O(n).
commonUseCases: Counting characters with utf8.RuneCountInString or len([]rune(s))
Treating binary data as []byte and decoding to string

commonMisconceptions.myth: len(s) returns the number of characters.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It returns the number of bytes. For non-ASCII text use utf8.RuneCountInString(s) or len([]rune(s)).

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can modify a string with s[i] = 'x'.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Strings are immutable; that won't compile. Convert to []byte or []rune, modify, then convert back to a new string.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Indexing s[i] gives the i-th character.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It gives the i-th byte. For multi-byte characters that byte may be only part of a rune.

visualExplorer.title: How `for i, r := range s` decodes UTF-8
visualExplorer.caption: Ranging over a string walks the bytes, decoding one rune at a time and reporting each rune's starting byte index.

config.intro: Decoding the string "a世b" with a range loop:

steps.name: Start at byte 0
steps.detail: The byte 0x61 is a single-byte ASCII rune. range yields index 0 and rune 'a' (97).

steps.name: Decode the multi-byte rune
steps.detail: Bytes 1-3 (0xE4 0xB8 0x96) form one 3-byte UTF-8 sequence. range yields index 1 and rune '世' (19990).

steps.name: Skip to the next rune
steps.detail: range advances the index by the rune's byte width (3), so the next index is 4, not 2.

steps.name: Finish on the last rune
steps.detail: Byte 4 (0x62) is ASCII. range yields index 4 and rune 'b' (98), then the loop ends.

steps.name: Key takeaway
steps.detail: The index is a BYTE offset, not a character count — that is why the indices were 0, 1, 4.

interactiveExamples.title: Bytes vs runes: len lies about characters
interactiveExamples.explanation: len reports bytes. For the two-character string "世界", each character is 3 UTF-8 bytes, so len is 6 but the rune count is 2.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: reverse a string correctly
interactiveExamples.explanation: Reversing the raw bytes corrupts multi-byte characters. Convert to []rune so each character moves as a unit. Edit the code so it prints the correctly reversed string.

checkpoints.code:
s := "héllo" // the é is 2 bytes in UTF-8
fmt.Println(len(s))
checkpoints.explanation: len counts bytes. 'h', 'l', 'l', 'o' are one byte each (4) and 'é' is 2 bytes in UTF-8, so 4 + 2 = 6. The character count is 5.

checkpoints.prompt: Which expression correctly counts the CHARACTERS in a UTF-8 string s?
checkpoints.explanation: utf8.RuneCountInString (or equivalently len([]rune(s))) decodes UTF-8 and counts code points. len(s) and len([]byte(s)) both count bytes, and strings have no cap.

checkpoints.prompt: This is meant to uppercase the first letter but won't compile. Why?
options: s[0] returns a rune, not a byte
Strings are immutable, so you cannot assign to s[0]
checkpoints.explanation: Strings are immutable, so s[0] = ... is a compile error ('cannot assign to s[0]'). Convert to []byte (or []rune), modify the copy, then convert back: b := []byte(s); b[0] -= 32; return string(b).

checkpoints.prompt: Iterate over the characters of s, getting each rune.
checkpoints.explanation: for i, r := range s yields the byte index and the decoded rune. Discarding the index with _ and naming the rune r is the idiomatic way to walk characters.

codeLab.title: Count vowels in a Unicode-safe way
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Solve(s string) int` that returns how many characters of s are ASCII vowels (a, e, i, o, u, case-insensitive). Range over runes so multi-byte characters never break your loop.
hints: Use for _, r := range s so you get full runes, not raw bytes.
Normalize case with unicode.ToLower(r) so you only test lowercase vowels.
A switch with multiple case values (case 'a', 'e', ...) reads cleanly here.

debuggingLab.title: Indexing a string returns a number, not a character
debuggingLab.symptom: Printing s[0] shows 104 instead of the letter 'h'.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Indexing a string yields a byte (uint8), and fmt.Println prints a numeric type as its decimal value — 104 is the ASCII code for 'h'. To print it as a character you must tell fmt it is a character, or convert it to a rune/string.
commonMistakes: Assuming s[i] returns a one-character string.
Forgetting that byte values print as numbers by default.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Print the first character as a letter, not its byte value.

theory.question: What is the difference between a byte and a rune in Go?
theory.directAnswer: A byte is an alias for uint8 — a single 8-bit unit of raw data. A rune is an alias for int32 and represents one Unicode code point (a logical character). A string is stored as UTF-8 bytes, so one rune may span one to four bytes.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two integer type aliases: byte = uint8 for raw bytes, rune = int32 for Unicode code points.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go stores text as UTF-8, so it needs one type for the storage unit (byte) and another for the logical character (rune).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Indexing a string gives a byte; ranging over a string or converting to []rune decodes the UTF-8 bytes into runes.

theory.whyImportant: Confusing the two is the root cause of most non-ASCII text bugs and a very common interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: Counting characters for a 280-character tweet limit must count runes, not bytes, or emoji and accented letters would be miscounted.

followUps.question: How many bytes can a single rune take in UTF-8?
followUps.answer: Between 1 and 4 bytes. ASCII is 1 byte; most other code points are 2-4.

followUps.question: What does len(s) return for a string?
followUps.answer: The number of bytes, not characters. Use utf8.RuneCountInString for the character count.

theory.question: Why are Go strings immutable, and how do you modify text efficiently?
theory.directAnswer: Strings point at a read-only byte array, so they are immutable: this makes them safe to share and slice without copying. To modify text you convert to a mutable []byte or []rune, change it, and convert back. To build a string incrementally, use strings.Builder to avoid repeated allocations.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Immutability is a guarantee that a string's bytes never change after creation.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It lets the runtime share string data freely across goroutines and substrings without defensive copies.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Operations that 'modify' a string actually allocate a new string; strings.Builder amortizes that by growing one buffer.

theory.whyImportant: Immutability explains why concatenation in loops is slow and why strings are safe to share — both are common interview themes.
theory.realWorldExample: Assembling a large CSV row with strings.Builder is far faster than repeated += because it avoids O(n^2) allocations.

followUps.question: Why is repeated `s += x` in a loop slow?
followUps.answer: Each += allocates a new string and copies everything, making it O(n^2). strings.Builder grows one buffer for O(n).

followUps.question: Does slicing a string copy data?
followUps.answer: No — a substring shares the original backing array, so it is O(1) and allocation-free.

scenario.question: A user reports that a name field showing '15/15 characters used' rejects their valid name early. Your code uses len(name). What's wrong and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: len(name) counts bytes, not characters. A name with accented letters or non-Latin scripts uses multiple bytes per character, so the byte count exceeds the visible character count and the limit triggers early. Count runes instead with utf8.RuneCountInString(name) (or len([]rune(name))).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A byte-vs-character mismatch in a length check.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: UTF-8 encodes many characters in more than one byte, so byte length overstates character length.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Switching the count to runes measures logical characters, matching what the user sees.

scenario.whyImportant: Byte-based length checks silently exclude international users — a real correctness and inclusivity bug.
scenario.realWorldExample: A signup form using len() rejects names like 'José' or '李雷' at fewer characters than the stated limit.

followUps.question: Could even rune counting still surprise users?
followUps.answer: Yes — some user-perceived characters are multiple code points (e.g., emoji with modifiers or combining accents). For exact grapheme counts you need a grapheme-cluster library.

coding.question: Implement `func IsPalindrome(s string) bool` that reports whether s reads the same forwards and backwards, handling multi-byte characters.
coding.thoughtProcess: Indexing bytes would split multi-byte runes, so first convert to []rune. Then use a two-pointer scan from both ends inward, comparing runes until the pointers meet.
coding.lineByLine: We convert to []rune so the comparison works on whole characters even for non-ASCII input. Two indices start at the ends and move inward; if any pair of runes differs, it is not a palindrome. If the loop completes, every pair matched.

followUps.question: Why convert to []rune instead of indexing bytes?
followUps.answer: Byte indexing would compare partial multi-byte characters, giving wrong results for non-ASCII text.

followUps.question: How would you ignore case and spaces?
followUps.answer: Pre-filter the runes (skip spaces, lowercase letters with unicode.ToLower) before the two-pointer scan.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Decide your encoding at the boundary: accept UTF-8 everywhere, validate with utf8.Valid on untrusted input, and keep raw bytes ([]byte) for binary payloads versus string for text.
productionDeepDive.performance: Use strings.Builder for incremental construction, avoid []rune conversions in hot loops when byte iteration suffices, and remember substring slicing is allocation-free.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Strings are immutable, so sharing them across goroutines needs no synchronization — a major reason they are passed by value freely.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Slicing a tiny substring out of a huge string keeps the whole backing array alive; copy the substring (string([]byte(sub))) if you must free the large original.
productionDeepDive.observability: Log byte vs rune lengths when debugging text issues; use %q in fmt to reveal hidden or non-printable characters.
productionDeepDive.security: Validate and normalize untrusted UTF-8 (utf8.Valid, unicode normalization) to prevent injection and homograph attacks; never assume input is well-formed.

caseStudies.problem: Character limits and search broke for non-Latin scripts.
caseStudies.solution: Switched length checks and truncation to rune-aware operations.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly more CPU for decoding, but correct behavior worldwide.
caseStudies.lessons: Bytes are storage; runes are characters — measure user-facing limits in runes.

keyTakeaways: A string is an immutable, UTF-8-encoded slice of bytes; len(s) counts bytes, not characters.
A byte is uint8 (one storage unit); a rune is int32 (one Unicode code point), and one rune may span 1-4 bytes.
Range over a string to decode runes safely; index s[i] only when you truly want a raw byte.
Convert to []rune to count or manipulate characters, and use strings.Builder to build strings without O(n^2) allocations.
